Concise Clinical Note 

Consult Summary:
• 65-year-old man with sudden painless left-arm paralysis, left facial tingling, dysarthria and mild dysphagia on awakening ≈1 h ago; high suspicion for acute cerebrovascular event (likely ischemic stroke). Emergency transfer arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint & timeline  
  – Awoke ≈1 h before call unable to move left arm; deficit persistent and painless.  
  – Concurrent since onset: tingling left side of face, mild difficulty swallowing (spilled drink), speech slower/more effortful; speech worsening during call.  
  – No left-leg symptoms, no facial droop noticed, no headache, trauma, loss of consciousness, discoloration or coldness of limb.  
• Past medical history  
  – Type 2 diabetes mellitus  
  – Hypertension  
• Medications: Metformin; Losartan; Amlodipine  
• Allergies: Penicillin  
• Family history: Father with heart disease  
• Social / preventive  
  – Lives alone. Former smoker. Alcohol: several pints beer on weekends plus a couple during week.

Examination:
• Remote (telephone) – no vitals available.  
• Patient reports persistent left-arm motor loss, facial tingling; speech noted by clinician to be slowed/dysarthric. No visualized facial asymmetry.

Impression:
• Working diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke – sudden focal neuro deficits, high vascular risk profile.  
• Alternate considerations:  
  1. Intracerebral hemorrhage – similar abrupt presentation; cannot be excluded without imaging.  
  2. Transient ischemic attack – less likely as deficits persisting and worsening.

Plan:
• 999 ambulance activated; patient instructed to unlock door, sit in hallway; clinician remained on line until EMS arrival.  
• Anticipated ED evaluation with stroke team for emergent imaging (CT/CTA) and reperfusion therapy assessment (thrombolysis ± thrombectomy).  
• No additional outpatient management given acuity. Documentation of PMH, meds, allergy conveyed/available for hospital team.

Quality checks
● Expected but missing: vital signs, objective neuro exam, blood glucose check, last-known-well exact time.  
● Transcript/DDx conflicts: none noted.  
● Transcript quality: clear history; limited by telephone format—no physical exam or vitals, some minor pauses.
